Spirit of Ubuntu - Christmas Special

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We meet three South Africans who unintentionally brought about the Spirit of Ubuntu.

Unique Selling Point:
Social media is playing a huge part in our lives - even moreso since the pandemic - and it often divides us... but every now and again it brings us together, makes us remember all we have in common and that at the end of the day we are all South Africans.

Summary:
Leo Prinsloo — Video went viral in May about the CIT driver that foiled an attempted hi-jacking seemingly without breaking into a sweat. Everyone in SA had a sense of solidarity about the crime we all have to face, that “Africa is not for sissies”… videos and jokes were shared over the internet and he became an overnight “Chuck Norris-style hero”.
Djo BaNkuna — aka THE CABBAGE BANDIT — BaNkuna was another “ordinary” South African that got people from all corners to rally for Justice for pavement gardeners. He was fined and threatened with jail time by Tshwane Metro Police because he grew cabbages on his pavement, feeding himself and those in need. it sparked a huge on-line community doing similar gardening projects in solidarity…
Sandiswa Kula — Kula is a photographer in the rural Eastern Cape who has also captured the imagination of many (perhaps not on the scale of the other two)… but she has gone where no other black, young, rural South African woman has gone before… She has changed the face (and image) of birding in South Africa… She’s a vibrant story-teller that goes out in rural Eastern Cape and … birds… She shares her finds and knowledge online, often wrapped in charming stories of rural life, but she is teaching and engaging with a sector that has traditionally been older white people who Bird as a hobby. And the people LOVE her. So much so, that Mark Anderson, CEO of Birdlife SA recently went to visit her.

Flights to East London for 3

Car Hire - Eastern Cape

Script:


SPIRIT OF UBUNTU -- Script FINAL

V/O
14
Social media plays a huge part in our lives, and even more so since the pandemic… it is a platform that often divides us… but every now and again people and stories trend, rekindling our spirit of ubuntu...
LINK (FB)
In May this year the name Leo Prinsloo was everywhere… Labelled as South Africa’s very own Chuck Norris, the security expert from Pretoria featured in a dashcam video that went viral overnight.
V/O
Alongside his colleague Lloyd Mtombeni, they got caught in the crossfire when an armed gang set its sights on the loot that Prinsloo was hired to protect...
UPSOUND VIDEO

Leo Prinsloo
Claire: When did you know you were in trouble that day?

Leo: When the shots struck the car.

Claire: What?

Leo: Ja. When I looked into the mirror I saw them, and I went for them. You know I was swerving into them and breaking hard. I wanted them to crash into me.
UPSOUND
They’re gonna shoot - they gonna fuckin shoot
Leo Prinsloo
Claire: When did you discover that the video had been posted online. Who told you? Where did you see it first? And what was your first reaction?

Leo: My brother actually sent me the video and it was that ice-bucket challenge. And I couldn’t believe what I saw..
V/O
Prinsloo ‘s level-headed Hollywood hero-style response attracted attention from far and wide...


Friends of mine in China, America, all over.. They contacted me like in 2 hours after I got it the first time asking me if I saw the video - I mean I saw it a hundred times already… but ja.. It was… it’s crazy

Claire: You became a South African hero. Everyone was so inspired… everyone was celebrating you …

Leo: Ja I don’t think it registered yet. It’s almost sad that something like that needs to happen to give somebody a little bit of hope. I think people are so hungry for something good to hold on to … that just filled that gap, probably.

Claire: So tell us, a lot of people don’t know how that ended. Did the bad guy get away?

Leo: Ja Unfortunately he got away.

Claire: Dammit.

Leo: Ja dammit.
V/O
But not all heroes wield guns! Some fight their battles through gardening...
LINK
When Djo BaNkuna first posted on social media about his pavement garden that was “under attack” by Metro Police, he could never have imagined the amount of support he would get from people all over South Africa… Who knew we could all be so passionate about cabbages?
Djo
In 2019 I started with the pumpkin, I had beautiful pumpkin. The biggest pumpkin that came out of here Claire was was about 8.5 to 9kg. I still have one of them still actually inside which I refuse my wife to donate. I told her I would divorce her immediately if she donates that one.

This pumpkin, we eat the leaves. Actually we eat the leaves more than the pumpkin itself. ….
V/O
BaNkuna has never been a fan of unproductive kikuyu lawns...
Djo
My wife had the habit of actually buying fresh produce to donate in Soshanguve so the idea came because it’s much more cheaper to plant vegetables than roses.
V/O
On the 9th of September Tshwane Metro Police knocked at his gate.
Djo
They gave me three options. Number one. Remove and plant grasses and roses. Option number 2. Seek permission. Option number three was just leave it barren like this and don’t do anything because this is municipal property. So I chose the option to go and seek permission from the council.
V/O
BaNkuna could find no evidence that the city By-Laws prohibited pavement vegetable gardens.
Djo
Djo: So, I put it on my facebook to say look this is what actually happened. You know, when I explained to people to say please, balance me here… “Am I doing something wrong?”

Claire: But then it took a life of it’s own … Everyone knew that there was a man planting cabbages on the street corner, needing to be balanced … What was your reaction when you realised that it spread to far and wide?

Djo: Took me actually by surprise. I was not actually expecting something like that, as well as I was not expecting the TMPD to really follow through on this matter because this was a non-issue.
V/O
Tshwane Metro Police slapped BaNkuna with the maximum fine - R1500… but thanks to the overwhelming support from people all over the world, The Cabbage Bandit did not surrender...
Djo
Djo: Without social media I would have been coerced to pay the fine and get a criminal record, So social media is very much powerful. I think it gives citizens a voice….


V/O
And it allows us to be inspired by ordinary people from all walks of life…
LINK
From the middle of the Rural Eastern Cape, photographer and birder Sandiswa Kula adds her own sprinkling of magic to social media.
Sandiswa’s Post
The Diederik Cuckoo image I took on Monday morning I think...I was doing laundry that's all I'm sure of. That is funny because the first time ever that I saw this bird I was also doing laundry….
V/O
At the beginning of Lockdown Sandiswa Kula moved back home to the Eastern Cape. Having studied Nature Conservation at Stellenbosch, she started photographing the birds in and around her village...
Sandiswa
so then what motivated you to start sharing a day in your life on social media?
Oh, that's a good question, because I don't think I ever wanted to share as much as I did. My life literally revolves around my chickens, my cats, my dogs and the birds that eat my chickens, and the fact that granny hates the birds because they chow her chickens. So I don't think it was planned out to go anywhere, but with everyone saying, Oh, this is amazing, this is nice. We enjoy actually hearing about something other than the city. I was like, Oh, let me just share with everyone else because I enjoyed maybe the people can live vicariously through me.
V/O
In between her daily chores, Kula finds time for birding and shares her photos and life, packaged in charming stories of rural life...
Sandiswa
Claire: You're hearing something?
Sandiswa: Yeah, that sounded like a red throated ringneck. I think I'm saying it right.
Claire: I don't even know where I'm looking, but I'm looking…
Sandiswa: No, the sound will tell you, I'll tell you, and it actually makes a call again. OK? They did it. Oh, yes, yes, it's coming from.
Claire: so when you go on these walks, you go far, how long do they take? You go every day.
Sandiswa: I would like to go every day.


V/O
And judging by the online support she’s getting, her followers would like that too!
Sandiswa
Claire: Do you think you found your community or your little tribe? Have you built a real, tangible network of people out there? Oh, that? Enjoy looking forward to your post, that comment, that engaged with you?
Sandiswa: Um, I think I have. I go bonkers over birds, and I'm not ashamed to admit it's I go crazy about them. Like, I would stop everything like, Whoa, let me get the picture and let me share if I can. If not, I'll share a week later and apologise because were like, we've been missing you. So I think I'm very happy and that makes me feel like I've found a place where I can be like, This is me, and no one is going to judge me for being the young one who's doing birding, the black one is doing birding, the black one who is the one from the village, trying to do something because if we're being honest birding predominantly would be a white person thing and you have to have money because the equipment is expensive, but you don't have to have the equipment to enjoy it.
V/O
And that, perhaps, is the secret to their charm… Three ordinary South Africans who simply followed their dreams and inspired us all to do the same...
Leo Prinsloo
Claire: It was nice spending time with you but it’s also nice to leave you without gunshots being fired…

Leo: I tried my best...




PROMO 1 11”
Three ordinary South Africans who followed their dreams and ended up inspiring a nation.
PROMO 2 21”
What do birds, cabbages and armed heists have in common? They are examples of how the unexpected can bring about the spirit of Ubuntu...
PROMO 3 21”
Rural village living, armoured vehicles under attack, and even a spot of pavement gardening. We meet three ordinary South Africans who became household names this year through the power of social media...
